teaser: Here the clouds are the heaviest thing in the picture, and the mountains flow like water.
review_notes:
Letter of early July 1889 to Theo: 'a blue sky like a piece of Scotch plaid', impasto 'like the Monticellis', wheat field 'which represents the extreme heat': check wording.
Cypress quotes ('beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk', 'a splash of black in a sunny landscape', 'not yet been done as I see them'): letter of June 1889.
Three versions: Met (painted first, outdoors), National Gallery London (studio repetition, September 1889), a smaller one for his mother and sister (private collection).
Met purchase in 1993 with a gift from Walter Annenberg, reported price 57 million dollars: check.
He regarded it as one of his best summer landscapes (Met).

lesson.text: Something is the wrong way around in this landscape. The clouds, which weigh nothing, are painted with the thickest, heaviest paint on the canvas. The mountains, which are solid rock, ripple like a wave. And the darkest object stands in the sunniest spot.

Vincent van Gogh painted it in the summer of 1889, outdoors, near the asylum at Saint-Rémy in the south of France where he was a patient. After weeks confined to the garden, he had finally been allowed to carry his easel into the fields.
What he found there was wind. The mistral, a strong dry wind, blows through this region for days at a time. You cannot paint wind, only what it does to things. So he made every part of the land bend.
Follow the wind from the ground up.

spots.title: The wheat
spots.text: The ripe wheat is laid on in short curved strokes that lean and swirl, like fur brushed the wrong way. He wrote that this field stood for “the extreme heat.”

spots.title: The olive trees
spots.text: These silvery green trees are tossed sideways. Olive leaves are pale underneath, and in the wind they flash almost white. Van Gogh mixes white and blue into the green to catch that.

spots.title: The Alpilles
spots.text: The blue hills are a real range, the Alpilles. He draws them with the same rolling line as the clouds above, so rock and vapor seem made of one substance.

spots.title: The sky
spots.text: Clouds curl into spirals. He told his brother the sky was “like a piece of Scotch plaid,” a woven pattern of blues, greens and whites.

lesson.text: Four layers, one movement. That is how the picture holds together: the same curling stroke is used for wheat, leaves, stone and air. It is also where the contradiction comes from. Run your eye over the surface of the clouds again.

Van Gogh wrote that the sky and the wheat were painted in thick impasto, meaning paint applied so heavily that it stands up from the canvas. Some of it was probably pressed on almost straight from the tube.

Everything bends, then: the field, the trees, the hills, the sky. Yet the picture does not fall apart into chaos. Under the swirling there is a very simple structure, and one thing in it does not give way.
See what stands against the wind.

lines.label: The top of the field
lines.text: The wheat ends in a near-level line. Below it, yellow. Above it, greens and blues. The picture is stacked in horizontal bands, like layers of earth.

lines.label: The hills
lines.text: The mountains rise gently from left to right, leading your eye toward the right side of the picture.

lines.label: The cypress
lines.text: One line refuses to lie down. The tall cypress shoots up through every band and nearly touches the top edge. It joins the earth to the sky like a dark flame.

lesson.text: That tree was the reason for the picture. Cypresses grow all over this region, and van Gogh was amazed that no one had painted them the way he saw them. He planned a whole series, as he had done with sunflowers.
For van Gogh the cypress was “a splash of black in a sunny landscape.” One dark vertical gives all that moving yellow and blue something to push against.
He compared the cypress to an Egyptian obelisk, a tall stone pillar, for the beauty of its lines. In the south of France the tree had an older meaning too: it was traditionally planted in cemeteries.

The green of the cypress is not really black. It is built from many greens, with yellow and blue streaks, the hardest color he said he had ever tried to get right. And low in the picture he hid its exact opposite.
A few touches of pure red are scattered in the wheat. Find some.

spots.title: Poppies
spots.text: Wild poppies, a few dabs of red at the foot of the field. Red is the opposite of green, so these specks, tiny as they are, wake up the whole lower edge. There are more on the left and far right.

lesson.text: He was pleased with this canvas and counted it among his best summer landscapes. So he repeated it. That autumn he painted a second version in his studio, now in the National Gallery in London, and a small one for his mother and sister.
The first one, painted on the spot with the wind in his face, is the one you are looking at. It is the roughest of the three, and the thickest.
It stayed in private hands for more than a century. The Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1993 with a gift from the publisher Walter Annenberg, for a price reported at 57 million dollars.

quiz.question: Which part of the picture has some of the thickest paint?
quiz.explanation: He painted the sky and the wheat in heavy impasto.

quiz.question: What does “impasto” mean?
options: A very thin, watery layer of paint
Paint applied so thickly it stands up from the canvas
quiz.explanation: Impasto is thick paint with a raised surface.

quiz.question: What is the one strong vertical in the composition?
quiz.explanation: The cypress rises through every horizontal band.

quiz.question: What did van Gogh compare the cypress to?
quiz.explanation: He admired its lines and proportions and compared it to an obelisk.

quiz.question: What are the small red touches at the bottom of the field?
quiz.explanation: Wild poppies, the opposite color of the green around them.

quiz.question: How did van Gogh describe the sky to his brother?
options: Like a piece of Scotch plaid
quiz.explanation: He saw it as a woven pattern of blues, greens and whites.

facts.text: Van Gogh painted this version in his studio, from memory.
facts.explanation: This first version was painted outdoors; the studio version is in London.

facts.text: He planned a series of cypress paintings, as he had done with sunflowers.
facts.explanation: He was amazed nobody had painted cypresses the way he saw them.

facts.text: The mountains in the background are a real range called the Alpilles.
facts.explanation: The Alpilles rise near Saint-Rémy, where he was staying.
